bio: John Irvine has been a steady Blue-team match-play piece from 2015–2025, piling up a 20-16-5 record (61.0% win-or-tie rate) across 41 matches while his handicap index has ranged from 5.4 to 16.0 (avg 9.3), which helps explain why so many of his best results come from formats where managing “the math” matters. His clearest calling card is Singles: an 8-3 mark (72.7%) with decisive finishes, including a 5&3 sprint past Kevin Rea in 2021 and back-to-back statement wins in recent years—4&2 over Brandon Byrd in 2024 and 4&3 over Ryan Quinn in 2025—both matches where Irvine essentially treated the opponent’s stroke cushion as a suggestion, not a plan. He’s also been hard to dislodge in the 2-Man Scramble (4-2-4 with an 80% win-or-tie rate), highlighted by a 5&3 with frequent running mate William Harris over Quinn/Jay Edwards in 2016 and a 2023 5&4 with Hunter Meriwether that never let a two-stroke disadvantage breathe. Tournament-wise, Irvine peaked early and loudly: 2016 and 2017 were carbon copies at 3-0-1 (0.5 points each), setting a tone of “halves are fine, wins are better.” His partnerships read like a practical toolbox—most often Harris (9 matches, 3-3-3) and Ross Montague (7 matches, 2-3-2)—while his rivalries add spice: he’s had the better of Byrd (8-5-2) and Quinn (7-5-1), but Mac Plosser (1-5-2) and Owen Mercer (0-4-3) have been the recurring reminders that match play always keeps receipts.

Louis Amagliani has been a steady Blue-team match-play piece from 2015–2025, piling up 41 matches and an 18-16-7 record (52.4% wins, 61.0% win-or-tie) while generally living in the mid-to-high handicap range (avg index 25.7, spanning 20.4 to 38.0), which makes his results feel appropriately “net golf, but with teeth.” His clearest edge shows up when the card is his alone: in Singles he’s 6-3-2, and when he gets rolling it’s emphatic—most notably a 5&4 takedown of frequent foil Kevin Rea in 2019, a match described as five straight holes won to start. He’s also built for rhythm formats, going 5-2-1 in Modified Alternate Shot, where patience and avoiding big numbers matter more than hero shots; the 2024 3&2 win with Ross Montague over Mac Plosser and Jay Edwards is a good example of “net efficiency” doing the heavy lifting. By contrast, Best Ball has been the stubborn puzzle (2-6-3), even with his most common partner Daniel Wynn (11 matches together, 4-5-2) and despite occasional scrappy momentum swings like their 3&1 2-Man Scramble win over the Quinn/Rea combo in 2021. If he has a rivalry, it’s Rea: 19 meetings and an 11-5-3 advantage for Louis—though Rea has landed some payback, including a 4&2 singles loss in 2023. Tournament-wise, 2024 stands out as his peak week (3-0-1), the kind of run that turns “handicap strokes” into “handicap stress” for whoever draws him.

William Harris has been a steady Blue presence from 2015–2025, and his 41-match ledger (12-21-8, win/tie 48.8%) reads like a guy who’s lived in the “halved on 18” neighborhood—useful in team rooms, less so for personal stat lines, especially with just 4.0 points credited overall. The clearest pattern is format-dependent: put Harris in a 2-Man Scramble and things get loud in a hurry (4-2-3 across nine matches, 77.8% win/tie), including a pair of tone-setting runaways—5&3 with John Irvine over Ryan Quinn and Jay Edwards in 2016, and 4&3 with Luke Jensen over Mac Plosser and Kevin Rea in 2017—plus a 2024 3&2 win with Irvine despite spotting Byrd/Edwards four strokes. Jensen is the signature partnership (11 matches, 6-4-1), and together they’ve also delivered in Best Ball, notably a 2023 3&2 win over Quinn and Owen Mercer with Harris effectively playing scratch while Jensen worked the handicap edges. His rival board is a mixed bag: he’s found a recurring handle on Jay Edwards (5-2-2), but Kyle Cummins has been a persistent speed bump (0-6-1), and Mac Plosser has had Harris’s number often enough to qualify as a long-running subplot (2-6-4), including the 2015 singles 5&4 loss and the 2022 Best Ball 6&5 drubbing. In singles (3-7-1), the volatility shows—none more brutal than Quinn’s 7&5 in 2024—suggesting Harris is at his best when he can turn match play into a two-man math problem rather than a solo essay.

Brandon Byrd has quietly built one of Red’s steadiest multi-year resumes, piling up 22.0 points over 41 matches from 2015–2025 (20-17-4) while riding the ups and downs that come with an 11.5 average index that’s ranged from 8.3 to 17.0. His best work comes when the match is simplest: in Singles he’s 7-4 (63.6%), and he’s similarly effective in modified alternate shot at 4-2-2, where halves matter and he’s been happy to bank them (a 75.0% win-or-tie rate). If his Best Ball line (4-6-1) looks like a soft spot, the tape has counterpunches—most notably the 2022 opener where he and Kevin Rea turned a handicap-heavy matchup into a 6&5 clinic against Drew Hursey and Daniel Wynn by winning the right holes at the right time. Byrd’s partnerships reflect that same practicality: he’s logged the most reps with Jay Edwards (9 matches, 5-4) and has been perfectly serviceable with Rea (7 matches, 3-3-1), while his lone shamble spin with Jay Snyder was a tidy 3&1 win. Rivalry-wise, he’s played John Irvine a ton (15 times) and has the scars to show (5-8-2), including a 4&2 singles loss in 2024, but he’s fared far better against Wynn (5-2-2) and Hursey (5-3-1), highlighted by a composed 3&2 singles win in 2023 despite conceding nine strokes. And when Byrd smells blood, he doesn’t nibble—his 2025 singles 6&5 demolition of Louis Amagliani is the kind of closeout that makes “press” feel like a bad idea.

Kevin Rea has been a steady Red-team fixture from 2015–2025, piling up 41 matches and 14.0 points (11-24-6), with a game that’s clearly more dangerous when shared than when left alone: in Best Ball he’s a plus contributor at 5-4-1 (5.5 points), while Singles has been the grind at 1-7-3 (2.5 points), a split that reads like “better in collaboration than in solitary confinement.” His peaks have been loud—he opened his career with a 3-0-1 splash in 2015 and then authored a perfect 3-0-0 run in 2023, highlighted by a textbook handicap-managed 4&2 Singles win over frequent foil Louis Amagliani, flipping an early deficit and never letting volatility into the match. Rea’s best partnership has been with Mac Plosser (4-2-0, 4.0 points), a duo that repeatedly turned 2-Man Scramble into controlled leverage golf, including decisive wins like 4&3 in 2016 (vs Daniel Wynn/Louis) and 4&2 in 2023 (vs William Harris/Louis). With Brandon Byrd (3-3-1) he’s been streaky but capable of outright blowouts, none cleaner than the 6&5 Best Ball in 2022 that became a hole-conversion clinic against Hursey/Wynn. Rivalry-wise, Amagliani is the recurring chapter (19 meetings, 5-11-3), and Hunter Meriwether has delivered both coin-flip battles (4-5-1 overall) and the harsh reminder of match-play momentum via an 8&6 Singles loss in 2022—proof that even with strokes, you still have to win some holes.

Mac Plosser has been Red’s metronome from 2015–2025: 28.5 points in 41 matches with a 27-9-5 record (72% wins, 78% win-or-tie), built on a handicap profile that lives in the mid-single digits (avg 6.0, as low as 4.8). His calling card is singles, where he’s a ruthless 10-1-0—less “grind it out” and more “end it by the turn,” highlighted by a 6&5 demolition of Luke Jensen in 2022 and a 5&4 win over William Harris back in 2015, both matches where he effectively made any cushion of strokes irrelevant by winning clean holes early. In team formats, he’s strongest when paired with Kyle Cummins (8-2-1 across 11 matches for 7.5 points), a duo that repeatedly turns handicap math into match-play momentum, like their 6&5 best-ball clinic over Harris/John Irvine in 2022 and a 5&3 modified alternate-shot rout of Jensen/Drew Hursey in 2019 despite giving strokes. Plosser’s tournament peaks come in waves of perfection—2016 (4-0-0), 2023 (3-0-0), and 2025 (3-0-0)—and his rivalry ledger is busy: he’s seen Harris 12 times (6-2-4) and Jensen 11 (8-3-0) and generally comes out ahead, even if scrambles can bite (notably the 2017 4&3 loss with Kevin Rea). When the format rewards decisiveness, Plosser tends to treat “dormie” as a deadline.

Ross Montague has been a steady Blue-team presence from 2015–2025, posting a 19-15-6 record across 40 matches (62.5% win-or-tie) while living in that very match-play world where halves matter and a bad hole can be erased by the next tee. His card reads like a format scouting report: put him in a 2-Man Scramble and good things tend to happen (6-1-3, a sparkling 90% win-or-tie), while Singles has been more of a grind (4-5-1), suggesting he’s at his best when the burden is shared and momentum can be piled on quickly. The partnership data backs it up—his most productive frequent pairing is with Luke Jensen (5-2-0), including the loudest statement win in the file: a 6&5 scramble demolition of Owen Mercer/Kyle Cummins in 2022 that “flipped almost immediately” after Red struck first, the kind of early reversal that makes opponents check the math twice. Ross has also built a long-running back-and-forth with Brandon Byrd (11 meetings, 6-4-1) and has generally enjoyed seeing Kevin Rea (4-1-1), but Mac Plosser has been the recurring speed bump (2-5-2), including a 2023 best-ball loss that swung on actually cashing handicap chances. Tournament-wise, 2021 was peak “never say die” (2-0-2), and 2024 was pure closure (3-0-0), a clean sweep that—like many of his best-ball wins (notably the clinical 4&2 in 2025 alongside Hunter Meriwether)—suggests Montague’s favorite scoreline is “this match never really breathed.”

Daniel Wynn has been a steady Blue fixture from 2016–2025, logging 38 matches (13-21-4) with a profile that screams “get me a partner” more than “clear the stage for singles.” His best work has come in the paired formats—especially Mod. Alt. Shot (2-3-2 with a strong 57.1% win-or-tie rate) and Best Ball/Scramble territory where he’s hovered around break-even—while Singles (3-7) has been the tax bill that keeps showing up. When Wynn and a teammate find the right rhythm, the results can swing hard: the 2020 Mod. Alt. Shot pairing with John Irvine went full no-nonsense in a 4&3 takedown of Brandon Byrd and Jay Edwards, and Wynn’s 2025 two-man scramble with Drew Hursey was a 5&4 runaway over Jay Snyder/Kevin Rea that never “breathed.” Speaking of Rea, Wynn’s funniest recurring subplot is that his most frequent high-profile opponent is also his most solvable problem: he’s 7-2-1 in 10 matches against Kevin Rea, including a controlled 3&1 with Louis Amagliani in 2021 and a 3&2 with Hursey in 2024 after Red struck first. The rivalries are real elsewhere—Jay Edwards (4-8) and especially Kyle Cummins (0-6-2) have been thorns—but Wynn’s peak tournament remains 2018 (3-0-1) highlighted by a composed 4&2 singles win over Reid Wesson after an early wobble. With an average index of 20.2, he’s at his best when he turns strokes into pressure and lets match play do the arguing.

Kyle Cummins has been a steady points engine for Red across 11 tournaments (2015–2025), piling up 21.5 points in 38 matches with a 20-13-5 record that plays even better in match-play terms (65.8% when ties count). His profile is clear: put him in anything that rewards teamwork and he tends to turn the match into a slow leak for Blue—Best Ball (7-2-1, 7.5 points) and Modified Alternate Shot (5-1-1, 5.5 points) are where he’s most efficient, while Singles (4-5-1) and especially 2-Man Scramble (2-5-2) have been more volatile. The Cummins–Mac Plosser pairing is basically Red’s comfort blanket: 8-2-1 together across formats, with statement wins like a 6&5 best-ball clinic in 2022 against William Harris/John Irvine and a 5&3 mod-alt-shot in 2019 versus Luke Jensen/Drew Hursey despite giving strokes. When Kyle’s cooking, it can get cartoonish—his 2020 tournament was a spotless 4-0-0, and in 2025 he and Plosser turned a “punch-for-punch” shamble into a 7&5 runway. Rivalry-wise, he’s solved several recurring Blue problems (6-0-2 vs Daniel Wynn; 6-0-1 vs Harris), but Hunter Meriwether has been his recurring speed bump (5-9-2), including a brutal 9&8 singles loss in 2023 that proves even a long-tenured point-getter can still have a round where the match is over before the turn.

Drew Hursey has been a steady Blue-team fixture from 2016–2025, piling up 37 match-play starts and a 15-17-5 record (54.1% when ties count) with an average handicap index snapshot of 15.9 that’s bounced between 12.5 and 20.0—basically, the kind of range that keeps opponents guessing which Drew is getting out of the cart. His best work shows up when the match is on his shoulders: he’s 5-4-1 in Singles and has authored some emphatic finishes, including a 6&5 in 2025 over Allen Bobango where he applied pressure from the opening stretch, and a 4&3 win over frequent foil Kevin Rea in 2024 despite conceding a huge net cushion—winning holes outright is a nice way to ignore math. He’s also comfortably effective in the 2-Man Scramble (5-4-1), and when paired most often with Ross Montague (8 matches, 4-3-1) the duo has shown they can convert advantages into daylight, like the 4&3 best-ball win in 2018. The rivalry ledger is where Hursey gets interesting: he’s handled Rea across 10 meetings (5-3-2), split evenly with Jay Edwards (4-4), and had a tougher time with Kyle Cummins (1-5-1) and Mac Plosser (1-5-0), which tracks with a 7&5 shamble loss in 2025 that got away fast. Tournament-wise, the extremes are classic match play: a spotless 4-0 run in 2017, plus strong 2-1-1 showings in 2018 and 2024, and a 2020 week of “never lost, but rarely won” (0-2-2).

Luke Jensen has been a Blue-team staple from 2016–2025, piling up 37 matches with a 16-19-2 record (48.6% win-or-tie) and an 10.8 average index (8.9–12.3), but his card reads like a match-play riddle: in pairs he’s a problem, in singles he’s been solvable. Jensen’s best weapon is the 2-Man Scramble, where he’s a blistering 8-2 and has authored some of Blue’s cleanest separation wins, including a 6&5 steamroll with Ross Montague over Owen Mercer/Kyle Cummins in 2022 that flipped after Red’s early flicker, and a 4&3 runaway with William Harris over Mac Plosser/Kevin Rea in 2017 despite Red getting a stroke. He’s also been more than functional in Best Ball (5-4), highlighted by a 3&2 win with Harris over Ryan Quinn/Owen Mercer in 2023 that leaned on steady net conversions while Red left strokes uncashed. The partnerships tell the story: Harris is the go-to (11 matches, 6-4-1), Montague is the accelerator (7 matches, 5-2), and even with Hunter Meriwether he’s 3-1. The rivalry ledger is wonderfully uneven: Jensen has essentially solved Mercer (8-0-1) and Quinn (4-0-2), yet has been vexed by Plosser (3-8) and completely stonewalled by Neely Mallory (0-4). His best team weeks—2018 (3-1) and 2024 (2-1-1)—hint that when the format lets him share the load, momentum tends to follow; when it’s Singles (1-9), the momentum has tended to follow someone else.

Jay Edwards has been a steady Red-team lever from 2016–2025, stacking 19.0 points in 37 matches with a 17-16-4 record that reads like match play is supposed to: slightly chaotic, frequently close, and usually decided by who cashes first. His clearest edge comes in Best Ball, where he’s 6-2-1 (6.5 points) and repeatedly turns net scoring into a pressure tool—most notably alongside Allen Bobango in 2023, a 4&2 closeout over Daniel Wynn and Louis Amagliani that never let Blue’s strokes settle in, and with Mac Plosser in 2017, another 4&2 where Blue’s early punch was basically their whole highlight reel. Tournament-wise, Edwards’ best runs came in 2021 (3-1-0) and especially 2022 (2-0-1), when he was banking points without needing dramatic rescue holes. Partner-wise, he’s most often been paired with Brandon Byrd (nine matches, 5-4-0) across multiple formats, a workmanlike tandem that can win but doesn’t always get the easy version of the story. Edwards’ rivalry ledger is fun: he’s been a recurring problem for Daniel Wynn (8-4) and Luke Jensen (6-3), including a vintage 2016 singles 5&4 demolition of Wynn, but William Harris (2-5-2) and John Irvine (2-5) have returned the favor often enough to keep him honest—see the 2016 2-Man Scramble 5&3 thump. When Edwards is rolling, it’s rarely noisy; it’s just holes quietly flipping Red’s way until the handshake arrives early.

Owen Mercer has been a steady Red-team fixture from 2016–2025, and his 14-17-6 record (16.0 points in 37 matches) reads like someone who rarely disappears even when the overall ledger leans the wrong way. His profile is unusually format-specific: put him in Singles (5-4-1) or, better yet, Modified Alternate Shot (4-1-2, a team-friendly 5.0 points) and he tends to turn match play into a slow squeeze—get a lead, make pars, and let the other side run out of holes. That showed up at peak volume in 2019 and 2021, when he went 3-0-1 in each event (3.5 points both years), and in one of his best standalone results, a 2022 Singles 5&3 win over Daniel Wynn despite “giving up 11 shots,” essentially treating the handicap math as background noise. Partnerships have mattered: with Ryan Quinn he’s a positive 3-2-1 across three formats, and with Tyler Blocker he’s 2-1-1, while his time with Kevin Rea is mostly defined by a clinical 2024 Mod. Alt. Shot 3&2 over John Irvine/Hunter Meriwether that never “breathed” after a three-hole burst. Rivalry-wise, Mercer has solved John Irvine (4-0-3) and largely handled Wynn (5-1-0), but Luke Jensen has been his personal bogeyman at 0-8-1—an imbalance that helps explain why Mercer’s one real soft spot is 2-Man Scramble (1-7-2), where chaos is king and Owen’s preferred brand of control doesn’t always get a vote.

Ryan Quinn has been a steady Red-team metronome across a 10-tournament span (2015–2025), posting 19.0 points in 37 matches with a 16-15-6 record that looks even better once you notice how often he turns matches into “no drama” outcomes (59.5% win-or-tie rate). His calling cards are Best Ball (7-3-0, a clean 7.0 points) and Singles (6-3-1, 6.5 points), where his ability to convert strokes into scoreboard pressure shows up repeatedly—most memorably in 2024, when he steamrolled William Harris 7&5 in singles, effectively ending the conversation before the turn. Quinn’s tournament peaks are loud: a 3-0-1 debut in 2015 (3.5 points) and a 2-0-1 run in 2022 (2.5) underline that when he finds a groove, he tends to keep it for an entire weekend. In partnerships, he’s been reliably productive with Kyle Cummins and Owen Mercer (both 3-2-1), and intriguingly unbeaten with Mac Plosser (2-0-2), including a 2025 2-Man Scramble win over John Irvine/Louis Amagliani that flipped a three-shot deficit into a 3&2 result. Rivalry-wise, Harris is the frequent foil Quinn has solved more often than not (6-3-3), while Irvine has had the upper hand (5-7-1), and Luke Jensen has been Quinn’s statistical kryptonite (0-4-2). If there’s a punchline in the data, it’s that Quinn thrives when he can play his own ball; scrambles (2-5-2) have been where his otherwise tidy match-play math gets messier.

Hunter Meriwether has been a decade-long Blue-team staple (2016–2025), and his 19-14-3 record across 36 matches reads like someone who understands match play’s only currency: holes, not aesthetics. With an average handicap index of 17.5 (ranging from 13.6 to 23.0), he’s been at his best when the format lets him apply pressure quickly—Singles (5-3-2) and 2-Man Scramble (5-2-1) are his clear comfort zones, and his signature performances are outright demoralizers: a 9&8 singles obliteration of Kyle Cummins in 2023 and an 8&6 runaway over Kevin Rea in 2022, both the kind of starts that make the back nine feel like paperwork. Cummins is his most frequent foil (16 meetings), and Hunter’s 9-5-2 edge there suggests a rivalry that’s been trending one direction even when it’s “close.” He’s also feasted on Ryan Quinn (4-1) while running into a hard stop with Neely Mallory (0-4), proof that every match-play résumé has that one name that shows up like a bad bounce. Partner-wise, pairing with Louis Amagliani has produced his best sustained team results (4-2), and with Luke Jensen he’s been even sharper (3-1), while the most common duo with Drew Hursey (2-4-1) has been more chaos than chemistry—especially in scrambles. Tournament form peaks in 2025 (2-0-1) and included a perfect 4-0 in 2018, meaning when he gets rolling early, Blue usually gets to count the point before the final putt drops.

Tyler Blocker has been a steady, occasionally sneaky-dangerous Red Team piece across four tournaments (2017, 2018, 2019, 2022), totaling 15 matches and 7.0 points with a 6-7-2 record that looks more middling than his best work actually is. With an average handicap index around 1.9 (as low as 1.0), Blocker’s game tends to travel in formats where clean execution beats chaos: he’s unbeaten in 2-Man Scramble (2-0-2, 3.0 points) and strong in Modified Alternate Shot (2-1-0), where he and frequent running mate Owen Mercer went 2-1-1 overall and authored a signature 3&2 grind in 2019 against William Harris/Daniel Wynn despite the opponents getting significant strokes. His best tournament was 2019 (3-1, 3.0 points), and he backed it up in 2022 (2-1) with a pair of statement wins: a 5&3 scramble with Kevin Rea where Red started fast enough to make Blue’s four-stroke cushion irrelevant, and a singles 2&1 over Ross Montague while giving away an 11-shot handicap head start—because winning holes outright is a good way to ignore math. Rivalry-wise, Blocker has done real damage to William Harris (3-2-1) and Daniel Wynn (2-1), but the one format he’d happily delete from the schedule is Best Ball (0-4), where opponents like Irvine (0-2-2 overall vs him) and Montague have repeatedly turned net numbers into small nightmares.

Reid Wesson’s Red Team career (2015–2016, 2018) is a compact 12-match sample, but it’s coherent: 3-8-1 overall for 2.5 points, with his best value coming when the format lets him press advantages quickly rather than survive a slow grind. His peak came right away in 2015 (2-2, 2.0 points), including a brisk 4&3 singles win over Sam Moody where Wesson (27.0) effectively made the modest index gap irrelevant by closing the door early, and an even sharper Best Ball with Brandon Byrd—his most frequent partner (4 matches, 1-2-1, 1.5 points)—in a 3&2 “nine-hole squeeze” against John Irvine and Ross Montague that never really let Blue breathe. Those same names define his recurring opposition, too: Montague (5 matches, Wesson 2-3) and Daniel Wynn (5 matches, 1-3-1) show up often enough to qualify as true foils, with Wynn in particular handing Wesson a 4&2 singles loss in 2018 by cashing a handicap cushion with match-play efficiency. Format-wise, Wesson’s most reliable lanes were Best Ball and Singles (each 1-2), while Modified Alternate Shot (0-2-1) and especially 2-Man Scramble (0-2) were less cooperative—proof that when the shot order gets restrictive, the match can get restrictive, too. Still, even in 2016’s lone bright spot, he was part of a 4-Man Scramble win (2 UP) over a Blue quartet featuring Montague, Hursey, and Wynn, which is about as on-brand as it gets for his résumé: do the damage early, and preferably while staring down familiar faces.

Allen Bobango has been a three-year Red-team piece (2023–2025) with a compact but telling 9-match sample: 3–5–1 for 3.5 points, hovering around a 12.8 index (11.5–14.0). His card reads like a format referendum—put him in Best Ball and he’s a problem (2–1–0, 2.0 points), especially alongside Jay Edwards, his go-to running mate (3 matches together, 2–1–0), where the two have repeatedly shown they actually know what to do with strokes besides “own” them. Their best work includes a 4&2 closeout in 2023 over Daniel Wynn and Louis Amagliani, described as a net-score clinic, and a 2&1 win in 2025 over William Harris and familiar foil Luke Jensen, sparked by Bobango cashing a net 3 on the opening par-5—momentum, purchased with handicap math. Singles has been more volatile (1–2–0), but he’s proven he can win the one-shot, no-excuses kind of match too, edging Jensen 1 UP in 2023 in a scrap where “wasted fewer holes” was the entire strategy. Jensen is essentially his recurring storyline (5 meetings, 2–2–1), while Hunter Meriwether has been a tougher chapter (0–2–0). Tournament-wise, 2023 was his high-water mark (2–1–0), 2024 a dip (0–3–1), and 2025 a steadier rebound—just don’t ask him about 2-Man Scramble (0–2–0), where the results have been as cooperative as a plugged lie.

Neely Mallory’s Red-team résumé is a small but loud sample: two tournaments (2020–2021), eight matches, and a spotless 7-0-1 record for 7.5 points, the kind of undefeated run that makes opponents start doing math on the first tee. The versatility pops in the format splits—2-0 in 2-Man Scramble, 2-0 in Best Ball, 2-0 in Singles, and even in Mod. Alt. Shot he never blinked (1-0-1), suggesting his game travels whether he’s freelancing or sharing swings. His best stretch came in 2021, a clean 4-0 sweep, but 2020 was nearly as tidy at 3-0-1. If there’s a signature partnership, it’s with Kyle Cummins: four matches together, four wins, and a perfect record across scramble and best ball; their 2020 scramble win over Hunter Meriwether and Daniel Wynn (4&3) was described as a one-way squeeze, and in 2021 they “cashed in” a handicap edge on the right holes to beat William Harris and Luke Jensen 2&1. Mallory’s rivalries read like a recurring Blue-team nightmare—4-0 vs Hunter Meriwether and 4-0 vs Luke Jensen, including a clinical Mod. Alt. Shot 5&3 alongside Jay Edwards and a singles 3&2 over Jensen where he leveraged his two strokes for early separation. The lone blemish is a halve (with Kevin Rea in Mod. Alt. Shot), which is less a warning sign than proof he’s human—occasionally.

Michael Edwards’ Ryder Cup-style résumé for Blue is compact but unambiguous: one appearance in 2015, four matches played, four losses, and 0.0 points, with a steady 24.0 handicap snapshot that suggests the sample is small rather than chaotic. He saw action across formats, but the data funnels him most clearly into team settings—two Best Ball matches alongside William Harris (0-2-0) and one Modified Alternate Shot with Ross Montague (0-1-0)—where Blue kept running into the same buzzsaw. Edwards’ most frequent on-course nemesis was Kyle Cummins, who accounted for two of his four defeats across Best Ball and Singles; the singles match was particularly bruising, a 5&4 loss in which Cummins “never gave [him] a chance,” stringing together five straight net wins from holes 10 through 14 and neutralizing any handicap leverage before Edwards could build momentum. In the team matches, the pattern was similar: in Modified Alternate Shot, Brandon Byrd and Kevin Rea “jumped…immediately and never let the match breathe” in a 3&2 result, and in Best Ball, Ryan Quinn and Cummins rode an early burst to a 2&1 win despite Edwards’ side appearing to have strokes “on paper.” If there’s a punchline here, it’s that Edwards spent 2015 trying to get a match to inhale—unfortunately, Red kept holding the pillow.

Sam Moody’s Team Blue career is a compact 2015 cameo—four matches, a 1–3–0 record—and it reads like a case study in how quickly formats and pairings can swing match play. His lone bright spot came in Mod. Alt. Shot alongside John Irvine, a tidy 3&2 win over Ryan Burgett and Reid Wesson in a match played “dead even” on strokes, where Irvine/Moody simply made fewer mistakes early and never offered Red a door back in; for a player carrying a steady 30.0 index snapshot, that’s about as clean a blueprint as you can ask for. The tougher side of the ledger is concentrated in Best Ball, where Moody went 0–2—both times partnered with Louis Amagliani—and both times running into the same Red duo of Mac Plosser and Kevin Rea, a recurring problem that twice “never let this Best Ball get off the ground” (3&1 and 4&2). If there’s a personal rivalry thread, it’s Reid Wesson: Moody split two meetings overall, winning with Irvine in alternate shot but then getting clipped 4&3 in singles, where a small three-stroke index gap still wasn’t enough to slow Wesson’s brisk closeout. In short, Moody’s data says he’s best when the ball is shared and the mistakes are rationed—and he’d probably like a Best Ball rematch that doesn’t come with a standing reservation against Rea/Plosser.

In his lone appearance to date (2025), Jay Snyder has already carved out a tidy 2-1-1 match-play ledger for Red, banking 2.5 points in four matches with a 75% win-or-tie rate and a steady 2.6 index that reads like a warning label. The sample is small, but it’s pointed: Snyder has been a closer when the format gets personal, going 1-0 in Singles and 1-0 in Shamble while splitting the “don’t lose it” formats with a Best Ball halve and a 2-Man Scramble thud. His best team chemistry showed up immediately alongside Brandon Byrd in a 3&1 Shamble win over William Harris and John Irvine, a match described as “simple match-play math”—few giveaways, timely birdie chances, and the kind of pressure that makes opponents feel like every par is on a countdown clock. Snyder backed that up in Singles with a 1 UP grind against Ross Montague, weathering the net-match-play swings and still finding a way to stay in front when the lead kept trying to change hands. If there’s one smudge on the 2025 card, it’s the 5&4 2-Man Scramble loss with Kevin Rea to Drew Hursey and Daniel Wynn, a reminder that in scramble, momentum doesn’t just shift—it sometimes gets repossessed. Overall, Snyder’s early profile is clear: give him a format where one or two disciplined swings win holes, and he tends to keep the point on Red’s side.

Buck Towner’s Blue career is just a three-match snapshot from 2025, but it already reads like a tidy match-play lesson in how quickly formats can swing momentum: he finished 0-1-2 for 1.0 point, with ties doing the heavy lifting (66.7% win-or-tie rate) while the win column waits its turn. His best work has come when the math stays close—he halved both of his non-shamble appearances, earning 0.5 in Best Ball and 0.5 in Singles, and showing a knack for hanging around long enough to make opponents check the dormie math twice. He split partners, halving a Best Ball with Louis Amagliani (0-0-1) but taking the brunt of a rough Shamble with Drew Hursey (0-1-0), where Mac Plosser and Kyle Cummins turned a “punch-for-punch” start into a 7&5 runaway despite Blue getting most of the handicap help—about as subtle as a concession you didn’t ask for. Rivalry-wise, Cummins has been the name that keeps popping up (two meetings, 0-1-1), while Buck’s other measured results include a Best Ball half against Jay Snyder and a Singles half versus Kevin Rea. With an average index of 9.2 and limited reps, Towner’s early profile is clear: stubborn to beat, still hunting that first full point, and probably allergic to shambles—at least until the rematch.

Ryan Burgett’s Red career is a compact, easy-to-audit 2015 sample: two matches, one point, and a perfectly symmetrical 1-1-0 record, with a 17.0 index snapshot that didn’t get the chance to wander. The split is format-driven—he was a problem in Best Ball (1-0-0, 1.0 point) and took his lumps in Modified Alternate Shot (0-1-0), which is a very match-play way of saying he looked a lot happier when he could make a mess on one hole and let a partner clean it up on the next. His signature result came alongside Ryan Quinn in a 1-up Best Ball win over William Harris and Michael Edwards, a match that read like an “escape act”: Burgett/Quinn spotted Blue three straight net holes early as Edwards’ stroke allotment cashed immediately (net birdies on 1 and 3), yet still found a way to flip the narrative and steal the point late—exactly the kind of swingy momentum that makes best ball both cruel and addictive. The other half of the ledger came with Reid Wesson in Mod. Alt. Shot, a 3&2 loss to John Irvine and Sam Moody in a strokes-even matchup where Blue simply “made fewer mistakes early” and kept the door shut. If Burgett’s rivalry list is short, it’s at least efficient: 1-0 vs Edwards/Harris, 0-1 vs Irvine/Moody—two matches, two clear lessons, and one tidy point on the board.
